scope: Feature flags in client apps and services: when to flag, flag types and lifecycle, removal, defaults on evaluation failure versus fail-fast config, naming and documenting keys, testing both paths, the provider-interface pattern and its standard (OpenFeature), vendor SDKs (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, ConfigCat, Firebase Remote Config, Microsoft.FeatureManagement / Azure App Configuration), local stores (UserDefaults, SharedPreferences/DataStore, localStorage, JSON), and platform-owner rules (Apple App Review, Google Play, Android, Microsoft, web).
research_type: Technology / software (Technical MEDIUM bar; one regulatory finding used as a case record)

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

methodology.method: guidelines/researching/process/research-methodology-and-sources: orient, go to authoritative sources (OpenFeature specification, platform-owner documentation and policy, vendors' docs for their own SDKs, the canonical expert article), chain citations, corroborate across independent sources, record provenance at generation time.
methodology.search_strategy: WebSearch for vendor and platform documentation on flag defaults, lifecycle, naming and local storage; WebFetch of every cited page; every quote then re-checked verbatim against the page text with curl (OpenFeature spec and Microsoft.FeatureManagement source fetched raw from GitHub; Apple UserDefaults read from its documentation JSON; the SEC order PDF converted with pdftotext).
methodology.inclusion: Primary sources first: the OpenFeature specification, Apple, Google/Android/Play, Microsoft documentation and source, vendor documentation for each vendor's own SDK, a government regulatory order. Expert secondary sources (Hodgson, Fowler on martinfowler.com) for the expert's-view question, which no primary source covers.
methodology.exclusion: Search-result snippets, third-party SEO blogs and governance listicles, mirrors of vendor docs, pages that could not be fetched (an Unleash unique-names page returned 404), and any quote not found verbatim in the fetched page.
methodology.scoring: guidelines/researching/evidence/verification-and-trust-scoring: Authority 30 + Independent corroboration 25 + Accuracy 20 + Currency 10 + Transparency 15, capped by the Technical MEDIUM domain bar (official current docs).

summary: Four of the eight rules hold: the injected provider interface (OpenFeature's provider model and Microsoft.FeatureManagement's DI both have this shape), UserDefaults on Apple, localStorage on web (vendor SDKs cache flags there; it is per-origin, string-only and can throw) and Microsoft.FeatureManagement with appsettings.json then Azure App Configuration (IFeatureManager still ships, though the docs now lead with IVariantFeatureManager). Three are contradicted: gating every feature (Microsoft says not every change needs a flag; Fowler calls release flags the last choice), SharedPreferences on Android (the Android team strongly recommends against it for new storage; DataStore instead), and fail-fast applied to flag evaluation (OpenFeature and every vendor SDK return the caller's default and never throw; failure belongs at setup, and flags are not config). 'Each spec lists flag keys' is unsupported: no source covers specs; the nearest practice is naming conventions, descriptions and a planned removal. The topic misses: a call-site default and no-throw evaluation, typed values, off means existing behaviour, no runtime dependency on the flag service, flag types with lifetimes, removing flags when done, unique never-reused names (Knight Capital), testing both states, decoupled toggle points, App Store 2.5.19/2.3.1 and the store bans on downloaded code, the local store as untrusted, no mid-session UI flips, monitoring rollouts, static config preferred, and a standard API (OpenFeature).
open_questions: Whether the provider interface should keep `isEnabled(key) -> Bool` or take a call-site default and typed values as OpenFeature does; the owner decides the rule's signature.
Whether to keep a 'spec lists flag keys' rule as a house convention; no external source supports or contradicts it.
Whether Apple App Review treats a feature already in the binary but switched off during review as 'hidden' under 2.5.19; no Apple text addresses feature flags directly.

Whether the fail-fast rule should be scoped to deploy configuration (where Unleash's config/flag split supports it) with flags explicitly excluded, or whether flag provider setup should fail fast as OpenFeature allows.
Whether the Swift guidance should name OpenFeature's iOS SDK or a vendor SDK as the 'backend later', and whether Kotlin should name Preferences DataStore or Proto DataStore.
limitations: The brief's 'App Store guideline 2.3.1 on hidden features' is out of date: the current hidden-features rule is 2.5.19; 2.3.1 now covers describing new features for review.
No Windows desktop (Microsoft Store) guidance on feature flags was found; Microsoft coverage is Microsoft.FeatureManagement, Azure App Configuration and Azure DevOps guidance.
No primary source speaks to documenting flag keys in a specification; the naming and description practice comes from vendors.
The web platform claim cites MDN rather than the WHATWG HTML standard.
Several Microsoft DevOps claims come from a 2022 page; currency was scored down.
The Unleash unique-names topic page returned 404; its point was taken from the Unleash best-practices page instead.
license: MIT (this research record); quoted material remains under its sources' terms and is quoted for verification.
